analytic.title: Partitioned and Overhead-Aware Scheduling of Mixed-Criticality Real-Time Systems

div.p: Modern real-time embedded and cyber-physical systems comprise a large number of applications, often of different criticalities, executing on the same computing platform. Partitioned scheduling is used to provide temporal isolation among tasks with different criticalities. Isolation is often a requirement, for example, in order to avoid the case when a low criticality task overruns or fails in such a way that causes a failure in a high criticality task. When the number of partitions increases in mixed criticality systems, the size of the schedule table can become extremely large, which becomes a critical bottleneck due to design time and memory constraints of embedded systems. In addition, switching between partitions at runtime causes CPU overhead due to preemption. In this paper, we propose a design framework comprising a hyper-period optimization algorithm, which reduces the size of schedule table and preserves schedulability, and a re-scheduling algorithm to reduce the number of preemptions. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of proposed algorithms and design framework.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION AND RELATED WORK
div.p: Modern real-time and embedded systems include applications of mixed criticalities. The mix of different criticalities originates from multiple requirements such as temporal requirements and safety integrity levels [15], [16], [19]. Very often, a mixed-criticality application environment requires temporal and spatial isolation to guarantee freedom of interference. Such isolation has traditionally been achieved by hardware design. For example, in many automotive systems, body control, brake control, and electric power steering applications all run on separate Electronic Control Units (ECUs). While such an approach has worked well in many industries, it no longer scales well enough to address the rapid emerging increase in new applications and technologies (e.g., active safety, advanced driver assistance, infotainment, and autonomous driving in the automotive sector). We therefore see a trend where a large number of applications with mixed criticalities execute on the same microprocessor.

To address the needs of isolation in modern mixed-criticality systems, the real-time systems research and engineering community has developed a number of schedulability analysis techniques and hierarchical scheduling policies. One very common temporal isolation approach in task scheduling is the use of a TDMA-based partition scheduler (e.g., ARINC 653 in avionics), where multiple partitions execute tasks on the CPU based on a pre-defined schedule table. Tasks execute within partitions based on fixed-priority scheduling (e.g., rate or deadline monotonic). This approach guarantees a certain amount of CPU time to each partition. If a task in a certain partition overruns, only tasks within that partition are potentially affected, and tasks in the other partitions remain unaffected as the partition scheduler guarantees CPU time based on the a priori defined TDMA schedule. As long as tasks with different criticality levels are not allocated to the same partition, such a hierarchical scheduling approach guarantees temporal isolation.

Related Work: Partitioned scheduling is closely related to server-based scheduling, where one or more real-time tasks execute on a server. Various resource models have been proposed for the analysis and design of real-time servers-for example, bounded delay [14], periodic [1], [17], [20], [21], and Explicit Deadline Periodic (EDP) [8]. These studies do not consider static server scheduling and they do not consider the preemption overhead, both of which, as we have noted, are important practical considerations.

Vestal [24] first addressed mixed-criticality systems by proposing a system model that has been widely used [7] and extended [3]- [5], [10], [11] in the real-time systems research community. The model essentially defines specific task parameters (e.g., WCET, period, and deadline) for each task and for each criticality level. However, in industry practice and safety standards, the perspective on mixed-criticality systems [12], [13] is that a task has one criticality level assigned, which is quite different from Vestal's model. While safety standards use different names to denote criticality levels-Design Assurance Levels (DALs) in RTCA DO-178C [19], Safety Integrity Levels (SILs) in IEC 61508 [15], and Automotive SILs (ASILs) in ISO 26262 [16]-criticality levels are correlated to the severity, frequency, and possible means to cope with a failure. Without loss of generality, we therefore use SILs to indicate the criticality levels of tasks [23].

Tamas-Selicean and Pop [22], [23] have proposed mapping and scheduling methods to minimize the development cost of mixed-criticality applications on heterogeneous partitioned architectures. Separation of different criticality tasks is provided by partitioning. However, the model they have used is restrictive and impractical: The major frame (i.e., the hyperperiod) is supposed to be given. This does not scale well with increasing number of partitions and change of task parameters. In addition, their approach does not reduce the preemption overhead due to partition switching. As shown in [18] and throughout this paper, it is important to reduce the length of the hyper-period and the preemption overhead in resourceconstrained embedded systems.

Contribution: In this paper, we address the partitioned and overhead-aware scheduling of mixed-criticality systems. To 1 isolate tasks of different criticality levels, we (1) synthesize partition servers and (2) generate schedule tables for the different servers. Our solution pays particular attention to the reduction of the hyper-period and partitioning overhead, where the key novelties of our framework are (1) an optimized way of server parameters selection to reduce the size of schedule tables and (2) a reduction of the switching overhead at runtime when switching among partitions. To our knowledge, this is the first work to build such a practical design and optimization framework to synthesize partitions and their schedule tables, while minimizing the overhead of mixed-criticality systems.

This paper is organized as follows. Section II presents our system model and preliminaries. Section III shows a motivational example, highlighting the problem solved in this paper, followed by the formal problem statement in Section IV. We present our approach in Section V and results from our extensive experiments in Section VI. We conclude the paper in Section VII.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: We consider a set of tasks Γ executing on a single-core platform. For each task τ i ∈ Γ, we are given the worst-case execution time (WCET) C i , relative deadline D i , and period or a minimum inter-arrival time T i . The deadline D i of task τ i is smaller or equal to its period or minimum inter-arrival time T i (i.e., D i ≤ T i ). The priority P i of task τ i is fixed and is used at runtime to schedule tasks on a given CPU or in a given partition. Further, we consider that each task τ i is given a criticality level SIL i (indicating that the criticality level is often determined by the SILs of the task [22], [23]).

div.head: B. Partition Model
div.p: One or more partitions may execute on the CPU. As discussed, partitions can be used to provide temporal isolation among tasks with different criticality levels. One or more tasks are allocated to and execute in a given partition. We consider that tasks of different criticality levels must execute in different partitions.

A partition is associated with a periodic server s i , which in turn is characterized by its capacity C si and period T si . The server behaves like a periodic task and executes for maximum C si time units within the period T si . The execution of each server is governed by an a priori defined schedule table, which is constructed with our proposed design framework. We denote the set of servers by S.

div.head: C. Server Design
div.p: In order to select the server parameters C si and T si , we apply a method introduced by Almeida and Pedreiras [1]. Their method determines server parameters for a given real-time task set to guarantee that deadline constraints are satisfied. First, a cost function C si /T si + C 0 /T si is introduced [1], [17], where C 0 is a system parameter indicating the switching time between servers. Through Almeida and Pedreiras' method, a search space of (C s , T s ) is obtained such that, for each point in the search space, the tasks within each server are schedulable. Selecting server parameters from the search space with the smallest cost function means finding the best balance between the server bandwidth C si /T si and server period T si .

By design, as long as all instances of a server are executed inside the time frame of their period, all tasks inside the server are guaranteed to meet their deadlines. In this paper, we present a static scheduling approach to schedule the servers. For task scheduling within a given server, we consider fixedpriority scheduling [2]. In the next section, we will through an example explain our application of Almeida and Pedreiras' server design approach.

div.head: III. MOTIVATIONAL EXAMPLE
div.p: Let us consider the example in Table I. The example contains 4 tasks, where the criticality levels for τ 1 and τ 2 , τ 3 and τ 4 are equal to 1 and 2, respectively. To avoid interference from different criticality tasks, we allocate τ 1 and τ 2 to server s 1 , and τ 3 and τ 4 to server s 2 . While the key conclusions of this example are general, we assume for brevity of presentation that the deadline of each task is equal to its period.

By using the algorithm proposed in [1], we obtain the server parameters (C s1 , T s1 ) = (1.3, 2.4) for server s 1 . Similarly, we obtain the parameters (1.4, 9.1) for server s 2 . Due to these particular server periods, it is not trivial to construct a schedule table for the two servers (the length of schedule table is large due to the server periods 2.4 and 9.1). By choosing the server periods to be integers, we instead get the following parameters: s 1 (1.1, 2), s 2 (1.4, 9). Note that the server capacities are changed based on the search space described in Section II-C. In this case, the hyper-period, which indicates the length of the schedule table, is reduced from 218.4 to 18. This in turn reduces the complexity of constructing the schedule table (due to the reduced range to [0, 18]). With increasing number of servers in industrial systems and a straightforward application of the method in [1], the hyper-period grows very large and further complicates the scheduling.

Let us now consider a scenario where we instead choose the server parameters as follows: s 1 (1.1, 2), s 2 (1.6, 10). In this case, the hyper-period reduces by 44.44% from 18 to 10. While such a harmonic period selection reduces the scheduling complexity and table size, we can observe that the total server utilization increases from (1.1/2 + 1.4/9) * 100 = 70.56% to (1.1/2 + 1.6/10) * 100 = 71.00%, which is only a 0.46% increase. This example illustrates the need of optimizing the server periods to reduce the size of the schedule table and the complexity of synthesizing it.

To construct the schedule table for servers s 1 and s 2 , we adopt an EDF scheduler to produce the schedule table for one hyper-period. The schedule of the servers is shown in Figure 1a. The white rectangle shows execution of server s 1 , the gray rectangle shows server s 2 , and the black rectangle shows the CPU overhead due to the switch from one server to another. In this example, each switch is assumed to take 0.4 time units (corresponding, in this case, to 10% of the smallest worst case execution time of tasks). Note that, in this example, we cannot construct a feasible schedule table within the hyper-period (i.e., the total server utilization for s 1 and s 2 equals to 1.1/2 + 1.6/10 + 0.4/10 * 9 = 1.07, which exceeds 1). This means that not all tasks within servers can satisfy deadline constraints. It also shows that although EDF is optimal with respect to utilization when switching overheads are not considered, it needs reparation for the case with overheads.

Due to the switching overhead, too many switches can make the system unschedulable, even for a system with relatively small utilization. By combining server slices, belonging to the same server, we can potentially reduce the total number of switches and reduce system utilization wasted. For our example, let us combine the first and second server slices of server s 2 . The schedule table is shown in Figure 1b. The number of server slices is reduced from 5 to 2 and the total utilization is reduced from an overutilized system to a utilization of 87%. The example thus shows that, by combining server slices, it is possible to reduce utilization due to reduced switching, and turn an unschedulable system into schedulable.

div.head: IV. PROBLEM STATEMENT
div.p: The inputs to the problem solved in this paper are a uniprocessor platform and a set of tasks with given execution times, periods, deadlines, and criticality levels, as defined in Section II. The outputs are as follows:

• Tasks allocation to partitions • A TDMA partition schedule T The constraints and objectives are as follows: First, all tasks must meet their deadlines (schedulability) and tasks of different criticality levels shall be isolated from one another by proper allocation to partitions. Second, we shall reduce the CPU overhead due to partition switching, and third, we shall reduce the partition schedule length.

div.head: V. APPROACH
div.p: The flowchart in Figure 2 shows our overall approach. Before starting to select the parameters related to partition and task scheduling, we construct one partition for each given criticality level (i.e., tasks with the same criticality level are assigned to the same partition). To schedule the partitions, we leverage prior work on real-time server design by Almeida and Pedreiras [1]; therefore, we use the term server to denote the partition interchangeably.

For the given set of servers, we propose a heuristic algorithm (Algorithm 1) to select the parameters of each server from the search space to reduce the hyper-period (i.e., reduce the schedule length) and to meet the task deadline constraints. After choosing server parameters, a static schedule table is constructed to schedule the execution of the servers. This may result in an unnecessary number of preemptions causing partition switching at runtime. Therefore, we propose a greedy algorithm to reduce the number of preemptions, which has a twofold advantage: (1) overall CPU utilization is reduced and (2) increased chances of finding a schedulable solution. If no schedulable solution can be found by the aforementioned steps, new server parameters are chosen from the search space and the process is repeated.

div.head: A. Hyper-Period Optimization
div.p: The method by Almeida and Pedreiras [1] to independently select parameters (capacity and period) of each server is briefly described in Section II-C. The parameters obtained from their method are optimal with respect to the cost function defined in Section II-C. However, if several servers need to be integrated on the same computing platform, their method is impractical due to the very large hyper-period, causing very long schedule tables, as already illustrated in Section III. The periods obtained from the aforementioned method are not of integer values, which makes it hard to construct reasonably sized server schedule tables. One straightforward method to address this problem is to, for each server s i , round the best period T best si obtained by Almeida and Pedreiras' method to the closest integer, and then through the search space described in Section II-C, a new server capacity C si is obtained. We call this straightforward method the Nearest Integer Solution (NIS) and we compare it to our approach in Section VI. Throughout this section, when a new value of the server period is selected, we consider that the corresponding server capacity is updated based on the search space described in Section II-C.

Periods selected by NIS are usually not harmonic. Nonharmonic periods of servers often make the size of the schedule table very large due to the long hyper-period, which may become a bottleneck in resource-constrained embedded systems [18]. In avionics systems, for example, server periods are commonly chosen to be harmonic [9]. In addition, the offline construction of a schedule table with a very large hyper-period is time consuming. Our HPOA algorithm is outlined in Algorithm 1. There are n servers, which are indexed by ascending order of periods and the period of the first server s 1 is rounded to the closest integer by calling the NIS method. The next step is to, for the following server s i , select a harmonic period T hm si (and by the search space of Almeida and Pedreiras also a new capacity C hm si ) from the following set of two period alternatives:

div.p: The harmonic period T hm si is selected among the two choices in Eq. 1 such that the difference to the original utilization is minimized (i.e., the absolute difference between C hm si /T hm si and C best si /T best si is minimized). If the system is not schedulable (i.e., utilization exceeds 1) under these new, harmonic periods (line 7), the algorithm continues in the while loop (lines 7 to 14) to divide the servers in groups to define new harmonic period relations to make the system schedulable. In each iteration of the while loop (lines 8 through 13), we first find the one server s j whose utilization is farthest away from the server utilization obtained by Almeida and Pedreiras' method, and then we divide the set of servers into two groups, where the first server of the second group is s j . The first group (s 1 to s j-1 ) is already harmonized. For the second group, we choose a new harmonic period by first calling the NIS method for server s j . The periods of the remaining servers of the second group are selected according to Eq. 1. In summary, the algorithm divides the servers into groups, each with harmonic periods, to reduce the utilization and make the system schedulable. The process outlined on lines 8 through 13 is repeated until the system is schedulable or until a maximum number of iterations have been completed. Thus, in each iteration, one new group is created by splitting the group that contains s j (all other groups remain unchanged) and then calculating harmonic periods based on the process we have outlined.

div.head: B. Server Scheduling
div.p: Once the server parameters (capacities and periods) are chosen within Algorithm 1, a static schedule table for the servers is constructed. Disregarding switching overheads, we know that the system is schedulable with the chosen server Algorithm 2 Greedy algorithm in Reducing Number of Preemptions (GRNP)

Since we are concerned with constructing a static schedule table for the servers, the first step of our approach is to initialize the static schedule table to the EDF schedule in one hyper-period. Thus, the initial schedule we construct is based on an EDF scheduler for the hyperperiod. However, this does not take into account the impact of switching overheads on schedulability and CPU utilization, as shown in Section III. Since this overhead cannot be ignored in real life, we propose in the following subsection an algorithm to change the position of server slices to reduce the CPU overhead and guarantee schedulability.

div.head: C. Reduce Preemptions through Rescheduling
div.p: Due to the nature of the EDF scheduler, each server can be preempted and divided into several server slices. Having too many server slices, each causing preemption and switching overhead, increases the size of the schedule table and therefore increases the required memory needed to store the schedule table. Switching overheads also increase the utilization and can reduce the number of schedulable servers. Due to that many embedded systems are memory, CPU, and resource constrained, it is therefore important to reduce the number of preemptions while still satisfying deadline constraints.

In order to deal with the aforementioned problems, we propose a Greedy algorithm for Reducing the Number of Preemptions (GRNP). We assume in the following that for each preemption, the preemption overhead is the same. The proposed algorithm is outlined in Algorithm 2. The algorithm starts from the second server slice and, in each iteration, it checks whether the current server slice can be combined with the previous (i.e., whether deadline and release time constraints can be satisfied if the slices are combined). If the check is successful, the algorithm combines the two server slices, and the procedure continues until the last server slice has been reached.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the proposed methods in constructing partition schedule tables that meet schedulability constraints while reducing switching overheads and the length of the hyper-period. All experiments are conducted on a desktop computer with a 3.40GHz Core (TM) i7-3770 CPU and 8GB of RAM.

In the real-time systems research community, two levels of criticality are usually considered, and, in industry standards (IEC 61508 [15], RTCA DO-178C [19], and ISO 26262 [16]) there are up to five criticality levels defined. Therefore, unless otherwise stated, our experiments were conducted on task sets with 2 to 5 criticality levels. We present 4 sets of experiments. For each experiment, task parameters are generated by the UUnifast Algorithm [6]. We assume that overheads between servers are set to 10 percentage of smallest worst case execution time of tasks in the experiments.

div.head: A. Hyper-Period Optimization
div.p: The length of the hyper-period is a key factor to be considered in the design of mixed-criticality real-time systems, because its value affects the size of the schedule table for servers. In this set of experiments, we aim to evaluate our proposed Hyper-Period Optimization Algorithm (HPOA) to select server periods.

Figures 3a and3b show the length of the hyper-period obtained with our proposed HPOA and NIS, respectively. As already discussed, NIS is a straightforward application of Almeida and Pedreiras' [1] server design approach. The results indicate that the value of the hyper-period increases as the number of servers increase. The results show that the length of the hyper-period is within several hundreds for HPOA, while for NIS, the hyper-period can reach up to 10 37 . Noting the scales on the vertical axes, we can observe that HPOA scales much better than NIS and produces hyper-periods (i.e., lengths of schedule tables) by more than 30 orders of magnitude smaller than NIS.

div.head: B. Impact of HPOA on Utilization and Schedulability
div.p: Our HPOA algorithm aims to choose harmonized periods for the servers to reduce the hyper-period and, hence, the length of the schedule table for the servers. In doing so, as also discussed in Section III, it may deviate from the server periods selected by NIS, which optimizes server periods for each server individually. This may imply that HPOA increases the utilization and potentially affects the schedulability as compared to NIS. In this subsection, we present results of experiments targeted to evaluate the impact of HPOA on the utilization and schedulability of the system. Fig. 4a presents the server utilization obtained by both HPOA and NIS, for the cases where the total server utilization is smaller than 1. NIS provides marginally lower utilizations than HPOA-however, as demonstrated in the previous subsection, at huge cost on the length of the schedule table.

For the 2 servers case, the difference in server utilization is small-always smaller than 10%. This small difference is because at most one server period is changed by HPOA compared to the solution provided by NIS. For the 5 servers case, the minimum and maximum differences, respectively, are 4.82% and 16.58%. We conclude that, in most of our experiments, the impact of HPOA on server utilization is small compared to its massive reduction of the hyper-period. Fig. 4b shows the impact of HPOA on schedulability. When the task set utilization is smaller than 0.5, all systems are schedulable for both HPOA and NIS (for both 2 and 5 servers). Therefore, to provide a better illustration, the figure shows the results for utilizations greater or equal to 0.5. The results show that the difference in the number of schedulable systems is small. As expected for the 2 servers case, the difference in schedulability between HPOA and NIS is small-always less than 10%. For the 5 servers case, the difference grows, because the chosen periods are further away from those that minimize utilization. This is needed to avoid excessive hyperperiods. The maximum difference is 16% of reduction, while the minimum is close to 0. We thus conclude that, in the majority of our experiments, our proposed HPOA algorithm provides huge reductions in schedule table lengths at negligible to no impact on utilization and schedulability. Only by such reduction of the hyper-period, it can be possible to implement these systems due to, for example, memory space constraints.

div.head: C. Server Rescheduling
div.p: We also performed experiments to evaluate the ability of our proposed GRNP algorithm in reducing server utilization. The GRNP algorithm reduces the number of preemptions between different servers by combining server slices together.

Fig. 5 shows the reduction in utilization achieved by GRNP. The chart shows on the horizontal axis the utilization of the task set before we apply our proposed framework for hyperperiod optimization through HPOA and server scheduling with GRNP. The vertical axis shows the reduction in utilization achieved by GRNP compared to the case where GRNP is not applied after the server scheduling step in Figure 2. As seen in Fig. 5, GRNP is able to achieve a reduction in utilization with the significant improvements for task sets between 0.3 and 0.6 utilization. As the number of servers increases from 2 to 5, the utilization reduction increases significantly (e.g., the maximum reduction goes from 15% to 26% as number of servers increases from 2 to 5).
Finally, as also discussed in section III, by using the GRNP algorithm to reduce server preemptions, an unschedulable system can become schedulable due to the reduction in utilization.
In our experiments for the 5 servers case, we observed that up to 30% of unschedulable solutions became schedulable after applying our proposed GRNP algorithm.

div.head: D. Scalability of Solution
div.p: Fig. 6 shows the scalability of our solution, for experiments with task set utilization equal to 0.5. Fig. 6a shows the total runtime of our design framework for different number of servers. As the figure shows, our framework scales nearly linear with the number of servers.

As shown in Fig. 6b, we also measured the runtime for different sizes of the hyper-period by running our framework outlined in Figure 2 with the number of iterations set to 1 in the HPOA algorithm. This allows us to evaluate the runtime of our framework without a proper hyper-period optimization. As expected, the execution time increases as the value of the hyper-period increases. The increase in execution time becomes dramatic and does not scale well for large hyperperiods. This again demonstrates the necessity of our proposed design framework.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We proposed a partitioned and overhead-aware scheduling framework for mixed-criticality real-time systems. Our framework, comprising multiple proposed algorithms (HPOA and GRNP), synthesizes server capacities and periods, schedules servers with reduced schedule length, and combines server slices to reduce the runtime overhead due to partition switching-all while maintaining schedulability of the system. Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency and applicability of the proposed framework to the domain of mixedcriticality real-time systems.
